Malicious and phishing websites remain one of the most common and effective attack points of cyberattacks, both at the individual and organisational levels. The sites will mimic authentic Internet-based services to mislead people to reveal sensitive data or malware code that instances a breach of systems. Old methods of site protection, including browser alerts, static blacklists, and signature-based detection systems are becoming less useful as they cannot identify the newly developed or rapidly changing malicious websites. Attackers often alter URL formats, domain attributes, and content of web pages in order to avoid detection causing delayed or inefficient protection.

The final system relies on engineered URL features, trust-aware indicators, brand-mismatch checks, lightweight DOM-assisted signals and optional VirusTotal reputation verification. The Gradient Boosting classifier was chosen after comparing the Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting models on the prepared dataset.

The threat assessment system translates confidence in predictions and supporting evidence into low, medium and high-risk levels. Low risk websites are allowed. Medium risk websites get caution notifications. High risk websites get redirected to a warning page with an optional proceed-once override.

The final architecture is a Chrome extension that communicates with a local FastAPI backend. This design supersedes the previous proxy-based direction, as it is easier to demonstrate, avoids the complexity of HTTPS interception, and directly supports browser-based warnings, blocking and logging.

The completed prototype demonstrates that a lightweight machine learning detector can be coupled with an automated browser response mechanism. It achieved good model evaluation results, maintained zero false positives on the curated hard-negative benign set for the chosen threshold, and passed the software verification tests implemented.

last_40_paragraphs: The results of these tests show that the system that has been implemented is able to correctly distinguish between malicious and legitimate websites, as well as having a low number of false positive results, and offering real-time responses to the browser that can be applied in real-time to protect users.
CONCLUSION
Summary

One way hackers trick people online is through fake sites designed to steal info. This work built a tool that spots those using smart algorithms trained on real data patterns. Instead of just reacting, it acts fast thanks to a browser add-on linked to a responsive server setup. Features pulled from web addresses feed into a decision engine powered by boosted trees. Depending on risk level, actions range from warnings to deeper scans via VirusTotal. All activity gets stored locally in a lightweight database for later review. Each piece connects smoothly - no gaps, no delays.
Key Contributions and Justifications

What stands out here is how machine learning detection links directly to real-world automated reactions. Rather than just showing how accurate predictions are, the system turns those outcomes into actual steps within a browser. For instance, it can trigger warning messages when risk appears moderate. If danger levels rise, access gets cut off automatically. Users still retain limited control through one-time overrides under specific conditions. Every interaction leaves a trace in local logs for later review.

Right off the bat, stories shaped how the system came together. Built-in web shortcuts keep things quick for live sorting tasks because speed matters more than bulk analysis here. Hidden structure hints plus name-checking layers slipped in later just to catch subtle differences others might miss. Heavy neural networks stayed out on purpose since simpler checks cover enough ground already.

Starting fresh, these choices fill holes found in past studies. Notably, there's a real demand for tools that spot bad websites fast while being clear about how they work. Instead of just flagging threats, the system pushes alerts straight to users. Built-in transparency helps people trust what happens behind the scenes. What matters most is putting usable defences into actual practice - no extra layers, no confusion.
Future Works and Development

One next step could be refining the prototype past its current FYP 2 stage. Expanding the data it uses might help performance down the line. Automated updates to that data, along with clear version records, may add reliability over time. Better methods for parsing page content would likely boost accuracy in detection. Looking into how redirect chains behave offers another path forward. Certificate details, too, hold clues worth exploring further. User privacy around log handling needs tighter safeguards than now. Outside reputation checks must also respect those boundaries just as strictly. Real-world testing across more diverse sites will shape its robustness ahead.

Putting it all together, the system ended up delivering a functional tool for spotting harmful web links. This version shows how a transparent AI approach fits into both a browser add-on and server setup, offering on-the-spot alerts during actual use - though certain boundaries remain visible, along with paths worth exploring later.
